title: Spartan Kid
author: Kyle Shepard
summary: Kyle Shepard takes his 6-year-old son Sam to a Spartan Race—a 1.5km obstacle course in the Poconos with 20+ obstacles—and documents not just what happened but what it revealed about Sam's character. The essay follows Sam from pre-race nerves (adopting 'I'm good' as his race motto) through genuine adversity: slipping repeatedly on muddy sandbag hills, briefly asking his dad to carry him, then choosing not to be carried. Sam finishes in the front quarter of 60 kids mostly older and bigger, but Shepard is more moved by how his son handled suffering: stopping to help another kid who dropped a sandbag, never complaining, adapting when he fell, finishing the second half faster than the first. The reflection: core memories like this one are the most meaningful work of fatherhood.
points: Sam adopted 'I'm good' as his race motto before the start after a Jelly Roll song—a mental cue they could deploy whenever nerves or fatigue built during the race.

On the sandbag hill, Sam slipped repeatedly and almost asked for help; instead he found different ways to drag the bag—forward, backward, along his side—making his own adaptations until he reached the top.
Mid-race, Sam stopped to help another kid who'd dropped a sandbag: 'First race, lot of perceived pressure, struggling on the hardest obstacle, yet still considerate of others.'
Sam finished in the front quarter of 60 kids, mostly older and bigger, by executing the race plan (pace early, breathe through the nose) and accelerating in the second half.
The deeper lesson Shepard drew: all we ultimately control is the attitude and effort behind our actions—and his son demonstrated the power of that perspective under genuine pressure.
quotes: I told him those kids were smiling because nothing feels better than overcoming a challenge.
We talked about how feeling anxious just shows you care and how the feeling of excitement and nervousness is identical in the body.
Proud moment for me. What a demonstration of character. First race, lot of perceived pressure, struggling on the hardest obstacle, yet still considerate of others.
He faced genuine adversity several times throughout the race. Despite straining, falling, and bleeding, he never complained, cheated, or mistreated.
All I know is anyone would be lucky to have a guy like you on their team. I’m really glad you’re on mine buddy. I couldn’t have prayed for a son better than you.
All we ultimately control is the attitude and effort behind our actions.
